data.title: The Riemann Hypothesis has been proven. Is the pie still safe?
data.description: A few days ago, the mathematics community achieved a major breakthrough in a century-old problem. On November 20, 2026, mathematician Levent Alpöge announced that, with the help of the artificial intelligence Claude, he had completed a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and published approximately 17 million lines of Lean code. This is of great significance, as the Riemann Hypothesis is listed as one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in Mathematics by the Clay Mathematics Institute, and numerous papers and theories are based on the premise that the Riemann Hypothesis is true. However, to be cautious, as of November 23, 2026, the Clay Mathematics Institute website still lists the Riemann Hypothesis as an unsolved problem. While significant progress has been made in the formal verification of the mathematical proof, the academic community's in-depth understanding of the proof's approach, and the formal review of the Millennium Prize, still have their respective procedures. Therefore, let's wait and see, everyone, and remain calm. But many marketing accounts are starting to use headlines like "The Riemann Hypothesis Proved, Bitcoin in Danger" to scare people. Frankly, I have absolutely no interest in opening them, but many members have privately messaged me asking if this matter really has any impact. To help you avoid the stress of investing, I'll explain it in the most roundabout way possible. Of course, let me clarify: I'm neither a mathematician nor a cryptographer. I simply believe that if something cannot be verified, it shouldn't be taken as imminent. Many marketing accounts may not even understand what the Riemann Hypothesis is, so let's start with a brief discussion. I also encourage you to find relevant videos to supplement your understanding with more details. Let's begin with a simple question. What do the numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13 have in common? Answer: They are all prime numbers. A prime number is a positive integer that is divisible only by 1 and itself. For example, the number 7 mentioned above is divisible only by 1 and 7, and cannot be multiplied by two smaller integers. Prime numbers seem ordinary, but they hold a very special place in the world of mathematics. You can think of prime numbers as the basic building blocks of the integer world; almost all integers greater than 1 can be broken down into the product of several prime numbers. For example, 12 can be broken down into 2 multiplied by 2 and then multiplied by 3, and 30 can be broken down into 2 multiplied by 3 and then multiplied by 5. In principle, every number, regardless of its size, can be factored into a prime number. This is crucial because prime numbers form the foundation of integer multiplication. However, this also presents a problem. What patterns govern the occurrence of prime numbers? Starting from 2, prime numbers seem relatively concentrated. As the number increases, the frequency of prime numbers decreases. Within a long range of numbers, you might encounter many prime numbers, or you might encounter only one after a long time. These patterns appear regular, yet it's difficult to find a simple one. Therefore, mathematicians are determined to find a method or pattern. They want to understand how prime numbers are distributed as numbers continue to increase. Can we estimate in advance how many prime numbers will appear before a certain huge number? This leads to the Prime Number Theorem, which, simply put, gives the average distribution pattern of prime numbers. It helps mathematicians estimate the approximate number of prime numbers within a large range, but this is not enough. We know the average trend, but we still don't know how much the actual distribution will deviate from this trend. Let's try to understand this with a real-life example. If you know that a city's average annual rainfall is 900 millimeters, then you know where the minimum flood control line for building a reservoir is, and you can then establish a reasonable reservoir height. However, for you personally, whether you need to bring an umbrella tomorrow, this 900 millimeters of average rainfall is meaningless. Therefore, the prime number theorem provides an annual average value, while the Riemann Hypothesis aims to answer the question of the range of fluctuation. And as mentioned earlier, Riemann himself didn't claim to have proven it; he only wrote "very likely," and then used this assumption as a ladder to derive a series of conclusions. In summary, the Riemann Hypothesis essentially sets a very precise constraint on the distribution of prime numbers, allowing mathematicians to further understand the extent of the deviation between the actual distribution of prime numbers and the average distribution. Why is it so important? Because prime numbers permeate almost the entire system of number theory. From integer factorization to various number-theoretic functions, and even modern cryptography, much mathematical research relies on prime numbers. If the Riemann Hypothesis holds true, it means that mathematicians can more accurately grasp a series of conclusions related to the distribution of prime numbers. So, after all that rambling, many of you are probably getting impatient, practically ready to grab my hand through the internet and yell: Will this affect the security of BigPie?! I know you're anxious, but hold on a second. We've just been discussing data science, while BigPie is about cryptography, which you can think of as a set of mathematical rules. BigPie's set of rules needs to solve one problem: how to allow others to verify your right to use a certain asset, while simultaneously preventing them from deducing the secrets you possess based solely on publicly available information. This is the value of BigPie's system, and the "core" that supports BigPie's future. The two most crucial concepts here are the private key and the public key. You can think of a private key as a key that only you possess, while the public key is a publicly available piece of information generated through mathematical operations. A wallet uses the private key to generate a public key. Others who know your public key can verify transactions you've signed, but they cannot easily deduce the private key from the public key. The elliptic curve cryptography used by Bitcoin primarily relies on a mathematical problem called the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. The name sounds complicated, but it can actually be understood through a simple process: Imagine you have a secret number. Following a specific set of rules, you can easily derive another public number. Calculating the public number from the secret number is fast. However, conversely, knowing only the public number and trying to find the original secret number using current classical methods requires an extremely high computational cost. This is the basic idea behind elliptic curve cryptography. Bitcoin uses a curve called secp256k1. The equation is very simple; all operations are performed within a range defined by a 256-bit prime number. The private key is a large integer, and the public key is obtained by multiplying the private key by a fixed point: Q = d × G. Simply put, all related calculations are performed according to a fixed mathematical rule, and the result is restricted to a definite range. Don't be fooled by the simple formula and explanation; the multiplication here isn't ordinary multiplication. It involves repeatedly adding the fixed point G along the curve d times. Using a doubling technique, the computer can calculate the public key from a 256-bit private key in a few hundred operations—negligible speed. Furthermore, note that this prime number is extremely large, with a size of 256 bits. So, if we're not in a panic, we should rationally ask: Since the mathematical tools used by PieCard are related to prime numbers, will the distribution patterns of prime numbers studied by the Riemann Hypothesis affect the security of elliptic curve cryptography? Again, I know you're in a hurry, but don't rush, because we need to understand another important technology of PieCard. Regarding encryption, PieCard uses two locks; we just discussed the first lock, and now we're moving on to the second. This is SHA-256. If elliptic curve cryptography is primarily responsible for transaction authorization, then SHA-256 in the Pie network handles tasks including hash calculation, blockchain integration, and proof-of-work, such as the familiar mining: Miners need to continuously modify the data in the block header, repeatedly calculating the hash value until they find a result that meets the network difficulty requirements. This process uses double SHA-256. A hash algorithm has a very interesting characteristic: a slight change in the input data can result in a completely different hash result. You can think of it as a special kind of digital mixer; whether the input is a sentence, an image, or an entire block, it can produce a fixed-length result. Deducing the original data from this result is computationally very difficult. Here's an interesting detail to add. The SHA-256 algorithm does use numbers related to prime numbers as some initial constants during its design. These numbers come from the decimal parts of the square and cube roots of the first few prime numbers, which seems to have some connection to the Riemann Hypothesis. However, these are merely fixed numbers chosen during the algorithm's design. SHA-256 does not require the Riemann Hypothesis to function, and its security does not depend on whether the Riemann Hypothesis is true. Therefore, we now know that the security system of Pie involves two important tools: Elliptic curve cryptography, used for key and transaction authorization; and the SHA-256 hash algorithm, used for data integrity, blockchain connectivity, and proof-of-work. They address different problems. So, back to the initial title: The Riemann Hypothesis has been proven, is the Pie chart still safe? The answer is somewhat unexpected. While there is indeed a mathematical connection between the two, it's not as direct as one might imagine. The Riemann Hypothesis studies the distribution of prime numbers throughout the sequence of natural numbers. One uses prime numbers, the other studies prime numbers. It seems like there's a deep connection. But there's a crucial difference: the Pie chart uses elliptic curves, requiring only a single, determined prime number and a set of designed and verified mathematical rules. It doesn't need to know how all prime numbers will be distributed in the future, nor does it need to rely on the Riemann Hypothesis to determine a prime number. The difference between the two is somewhat like not classifying nail trimming as a surgical procedure, although it might seem somewhat related. Therefore, you can remember this: BigPie's cryptography uses mathematical tools related to prime numbers, but its security is not based on the premise that the Riemann Hypothesis is true. Or, from a discussion perspective, what would happen to BigPie if the Riemann Hypothesis were formally proven, or one day disproven? First, let's assume the Riemann Hypothesis is eventually proven true. This means mathematicians will have a more solid theoretical foundation for understanding the distribution of prime numbers, leading to significant progress in mathematical research and potentially further refining algorithmic analysis that relies on related number theory conclusions. However, for Pie, this won't automatically grant it greater security. Your private key won't become longer, your public key won't change, and SHA-256 won't suddenly become more secure because the Riemann Hypothesis is proven. Pie's existing consensus rules, cryptographic parameters, and transaction verification methods won't automatically change because of this mathematical proof. So, what if the situation were reversed? Suppose that mathematicians eventually discover that the Riemann Hypothesis is wrong, finding a counterexample that does not conform to the original conjecture. This would indeed be a major event in the history of mathematics. Many theoretical conclusions relying on the Riemann Hypothesis would need to be re-examined, and the research directions of some mathematicians might change as a result. However, this still does not directly lead to the conclusion that the cryptographic system of the Riemann Hypothesis has been compromised, because proving the Riemann Hypothesis is wrong and finding an algorithm that can quickly solve the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem are two different things. Only when subsequent research discovers a new, exploitable algorithm that can effectively attack existing cryptographic systems under realistic computational conditions will a real security threat be posed. As of now, progress in proving the Riemann Hypothesis has not yielded such a conclusion. Therefore, whether the Riemann Hypothesis is proven true or ultimately disproven, we cannot conclude that Pyramid's security will change based solely on this one event. I've written a bit too much, so let me end with a reminder: whether you're a veteran in the crypto space like me since 2017, or a newbie who's just entered the field, you need to understand that cryptographic security and asset management security are two issues that need to be considered separately. Looking back, the Riemann Hypothesis remains an extremely important mathematical problem, studying the patterns behind prime numbers and helping humanity further understand the digital world. The Pie, on the other hand, is a system that combines mathematics, cryptography, computer networks, and economic incentives. There is mathematical overlap between the two, but they also have their own independent research problems. We should certainly pay attention to advancements in mathematics and technology, especially breakthroughs that may change the existing boundaries of cryptographic security. However, there's no need to worry about whether your wallet will be able to open tomorrow just because a mathematical problem has been solved. Understanding the boundaries of technology is far more important than panicking at the sound of a new term. Please verify, do not believe. This statement applies to investing, and it also applies to the technical field. 1 BTC = 1 BTC. At least today, the progress in proving the Riemann Hypothesis has not changed this. Security should come from understanding the hypothesis, not from associations with its name. Wishing everyone a good mindset to navigate through cycles.

data.title: Chainflip Confirms $12 Million Crypto Hack After Bitcoin and Ethereum Vaults Are Drained, Offers Hacker $1.2 Million to Return Stolen Funds
data.description:
Chainflip is offering an attacker a $1.2 million reward to return most of the $12 million stolen from its cross-chain vaults, as the protocol attempts to recover funds and limit further damage following the exploit.

The attacker has until 18:38 UTC on 23 November 2026 to return 90% of the stolen assets, with Chainflip promising to allow the hacker to keep the remaining 10% as a bounty.

The company said it would classify the incident as a white-hat recovery and withdraw its law enforcement complaints if the funds were returned before the deadline.

We have sent an on-chain message to the address holding the BTC taken from Chainflip on 21 November.

Offer: return 90% of the funds, keep 10% as a bounty. Terms and return addresses: https://t.co/hspHwh43lw

Tx: https://t.co/NrYEeZFMxD

The offer is open until 18:38 UTC on 23…

— CHAINFLIP (@Chainflip) November 21, 2026

Chainflip Confirms $12 Million Loss Across Bitcoin, Ethereum and Stablecoin Vaults

Chainflip Labs, the operator of the cross-chain decentralised exchange, confirmed that attackers stole 122.86 Bitcoin (BTC), 520.22 Ether (ETH), 3.25 million USDC and 758,141 USDT in the 21 November 2026 incident.

The confirmed losses are substantially higher than the initial estimate of $4.86 million, which covered assets drained from an Ethereum vault.

Chainflip (@Chainflip) was hacked for 4.86M!

Thestolenfundsinclude3.25MUSDC, 520.22 ETH(851K), and 758K USDT.

Thehackerhasalreadyswappedallthestolenfundsfor2,910ETH (4.76M)anddepositedtheETH into #TornadoCash.https://t.co/ZzOMJZaY8F… pic.twitter.com/d0ooM4uhxp

— Lookonchain (@lookonchain) November 21, 2026

Further investigations uncovered another $7.1 million in Bitcoin stolen from a separate Bitcoin vault, bringing the total losses to approximately $12 million.

The scale of the incident is particularly concerning given the protocol's relatively small reserves.

According to DeFiLlama, Chainflip's total value locked (TVL) stood at approximately $14.45 million a week before the attack, meaning the stolen assets represented more than 80% of that figure.

Chainflip's native FLIP token also suffered heavy losses following the incident.

According to CoinGecko data, the token fell as much as 42.9% over 24 hours, while subsequent reports placed its decline at around 37%.

How Did the Attacker Gain Access to Chainflip's Vaults?

Chainflip traced preparations for the attack to 11 November, when the attacker allegedly funded activity through Tornado Cash, followed by a FLIP token purchase and the registration of a validator account on 20 November.

According to DeFiLlama's hack database, the attacker exploited Chainflip's aggregate validator signing key by using a valid Schnorr signature with an unusual nonce outside the protocol's normal signing sequence.

This enabled the attacker to drain assets from the Ethereum vault.

The stolen stablecoins were subsequently converted into Ether, with approximately 2,909 ETH transferred to Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service used to obscure transaction trails.

CHAINFLIP HIT BY 4.86MEXPLOIT,HACKERLAUNDERSETHTHROUGHTORNADOCASH

Anattackerdrained520.2ETH, 3.25M USDC and 758K USDT (~$4.86M) from Chainflip's Ethereum vault.

The exploit involved a valid signature from the vault's aggregate signing key, suggesting a private key… pic.twitter.com/F8qxDULnax

— Onchain Lens (@OnchainLens) November 21, 2026

Chainflip has since identified the mechanism behind the cryptographic key exposure and said it had taken steps to prevent similar incidents.

However, the exact technical details of the vulnerability have not been fully disclosed.

The protocol's security structure relies on validators jointly managing a signing key.

Its system can involve up to 150 validators, with at least 100 required to approve transactions, making the potential compromise of its shared signing infrastructure a central concern.

A valid signature is not a safe transaction.

Chainflip paid out on a signature that matched the live key but carried an out-of-sequence nonce. The check passed. The vault still emptied.

Verifying who signed is not enough. Something has to check what is being signed (nonce,…

— 0xki (@W3B_AI_SR) November 23, 2026

Chainflip Warns Attacker as It Offers 10% Bounty

Alongside its investigation, Chainflip issued a direct message to the attacker, offering to treat the return of 90% of the stolen assets as a white-hat recovery rather than pursuing the individual through law enforcement.

The company set the deadline at 18:38 UTC on 23 November, offering the attacker approximately $1.2 million worth of assets in exchange for returning the remaining funds.

Chainflip also identified the wallets designated to receive the recovered Bitcoin and Ether, which correspond to the safe-return addresses listed in its bug bounty policy.

The company warned that it had obtained identifying information connected to the validator and servers involved in the attack, while the associated wallet addresses had been flagged by major blockchain analytics firms.

Chainflip said,

“We hold identifying information on the validator and servers used, your addresses are flagged across every major analytics firm, and every Tornado Cash withdrawal is being watched.”

The company added that it would withdraw its reports and complaints to law enforcement if the attacker met the recovery conditions before the deadline.

Service Remains Suspended as Chainflip Reviews Compensation

Chainflip has suspended its service following the exploit while it works to secure its infrastructure and investigate the full extent of the damage.

Founder Simon Harman said he is cooperating with law enforcement and investigators, while acknowledging the financial impact on liquidity providers.

“Liquidity providers have suffered substantial losses, but I am relatively confident that we will be able to resume the service.”

Quick update on the @Chainflip situation: I've been in contact with all of our stakeholders, team, and external law enforcement and investigative organisations since the incident yesterday and we've all been working hard to do what needs to be done in the immediate aftermath.…

— Simon Harman 🫵 (@SimonAHarman) November 22, 2026

The company is also reviewing possible compensation arrangements for affected liquidity providers as it assesses the damage and considers how to restore operations.

Although Chainflip has identified the mechanism behind the attack and secured information that could help investigators trace the attacker, the recovery of the stolen assets remains uncertain.

data.title: Hong Kong CARF Launch: Tighter Taxation for Crypto Enthusiasts – Are There Risks in Withdrawing Funds for Crypto Trading?
data.description:
Hong Kong is advancing its Crypto Asset Reporting Framework (CARF), planning to collect crypto asset transaction information starting in 2027 and launch related reporting and cross-border information exchange in 2028. This news has sparked widespread discussion in the Chinese crypto community, even triggering some panic. This episode of "Wu Says No Crypto" invites FinTax founder Calix to explain the differences between CARF and traditional CRS and exchange KYC, and how the new regulations will affect Hong Kong and overseas exchanges, crypto investors, and Web3 practitioners. Calix points out that the core of CARF is to allow different tax jurisdictions to exchange crypto asset transaction information, and the reporting obligation does not entirely depend on whether the exchange is licensed or registered in which country. Regarding the tax issues that investors are most concerned about, Calix explained that although transactions before 2027 are not within the scope of the first round of transaction information collection by Hong Kong CARF, this does not mean that historical assets and income are automatically exempt from tax audits. Crypto assets accumulated before 2027 may still be subject to reporting when transferred or exchanged after 2027. Hong Kong does not have a capital gains tax, but crypto assets obtained through business activities or remuneration may still be subject to profits tax or salaries tax. For individuals who have moved from mainland China to Hong Kong, obtaining Hong Kong residency does not automatically mean losing mainland tax residency; specific tax obligations still depend on the actual circumstances. The interview also discussed the impact of mainland China not yet joining CARF, whether cryptocurrency withdrawals through Hong Kong bank cards will leave tax records, and whether historical income may be retroactively pursued in the future. Calix believes that even if crypto transaction information is not yet exchanged with mainland China through CARF, Hong Kong bank accounts may still be subject to CRS information exchange. However, there is still uncertainty regarding mainland China's crypto asset tax rules, the scope of future audits, and the retrospective period. He suggests that Web3 practitioners and high-net-worth investors should proactively review their asset sources, transaction records, and tax residency status, rather than waiting until regulations are implemented to address historical issues. What are the differences between CARF, CRS, and KYC? What information do investors need to declare? AKI: Hong Kong plans to start collecting crypto asset transaction information from 2027. What exactly is CARF? How does it differ from traditional CRS and exchange KYC? Calix: CARF (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework) can be understood as the CRS for the crypto asset field. It primarily targets qualified crypto asset service providers, namely RCASP (Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Providers). These institutions are required to collect user identity and transaction information and report it to the local tax authorities as required. The tax authorities then exchange information with other participating jurisdictions based on the user's tax residency status. While CRS mainly covers traditional financial accounts such as banks and securities firms, CARF extends information exchange to crypto asset transactions. KYC is the basic procedure for platforms to identify customers, while CARF further requires platforms to collect tax residency information and related transaction data, and to fulfill tax reporting obligations. AKI: What specific obligations are added for investors and trading platforms? Calix: Investors first need to provide the platform with self-verification of their tax residency. If there is a significant change in their residency, the platform is also responsible for re-verification. The platform then needs to combine KYC, tax residency information, and transaction records to complete the annual CARF report. For investors, the biggest change is that tax authorities may obtain their cryptocurrency transaction records through cross-border information exchange and further inquire about the source of assets, the nature of income, and tax payment status. It's important to note that CARF itself is not a new tax system, but rather an information collection and exchange mechanism. Whether or not taxes need to be paid, and at what tax rate, still depends on the existing tax laws of each region. Will CARF weaken Hong Kong's competitiveness in the crypto space? Will offshore exchanges be affected? AKI: Hong Kong has been actively developing its crypto industry in recent years. Will CARF weaken Hong Kong's competitiveness relative to financial centers like Singapore? Calix: I believe the impact will be limited. CARF is an international tax cooperation framework, and major financial centers are gradually establishing similar information exchange systems. The international tax transparency requirements faced by financial centers such as Hong Kong, Singapore, and London are not fundamentally different. For Hong Kong, participating in CARF means both providing relevant tax information to other regions and gaining access to the transaction records of Hong Kong tax residents on overseas platforms. In the long run, systems such as anti-money laundering, KYC, CRS, and CARF help improve the transparency of financial activities. I don't believe CARF will significantly weaken Hong Kong's competitiveness as a financial center. AKI: Does CARF only apply to licensed exchanges in Hong Kong? If an exchange is registered overseas, is it exempt from reporting? Calix: CARF and exchange licensing are two different systems. Whether reporting is required depends primarily on whether the institution meets the RCASP definition and complies with local Nexus Rules, not just whether it has a license. For example, a company registered in the BVI but with its actual management team, principal activities, or place of business located in Hong Kong may have sufficient tax connection with Hong Kong to incur CARF reporting obligations. For users, tax residency is equally important. If a Hong Kong tax resident trades on a European platform, their transaction information may be exchanged with Hong Kong through European tax authorities if relevant information exchange arrangements are in place there. Using a Hong Kong-based platform may also incur local reporting obligations. Therefore, it cannot be simply assumed that using offshore exchanges will avoid CARF. In the future, transaction information from different platforms may gradually be aggregated in the user's tax jurisdiction. Will transactions and positions before 2027 be retroactively taxed? AKI: Hong Kong plans to start collecting transaction information from 2027 and launch reporting and exchange in 2028. How will transactions and positions before that be handled? Calix: According to the currently discussed implementation arrangements, transactions occurring before 2027 are not within the scope of the first round of CARF transaction information collection. However, it's important to distinguish between historical transactions and historical assets. For example, if someone accumulated a large amount of BTC before 2027, these historical transactions themselves will not be automatically included in the first round of reporting due to the launch of CARF. However, if the relevant assets are transferred, exchanged, or sold after 2027, the new transactions may be included in the reporting scope. More importantly, CARF's non-retroactive collection of historical transactions does not mean that historical gains are automatically tax-exempt. If the tax authorities discover that an account has a large amount of historically accumulated crypto assets, they may still require an explanation of the source and acquisition method of the assets, as well as whether there was taxable income previously, based on existing tax laws. Therefore, 2027 is not a tax-related starting point for clearing or recalculating assets. Whether historical assets involve tax obligations depends on the applicable law at the time of acquisition. Hong Kong does not have a capital gains tax; are cryptocurrency gains still taxable? AKI: Hong Kong does not have a capital gains tax, so are investors exempt from taxing gains from trading crypto assets? Calix: It can't be generalized. Hong Kong doesn't have a capital gains tax, but it still has profits tax and salaries tax; the key is the nature of the income. If an individual holds crypto assets long-term, the proceeds from the sale are considered capital gains and usually don't involve capital gains tax. However, if the transaction constitutes a business transaction, the profits generated may fall under the scope of profits tax. The standard profits tax rate for Hong Kong corporations is 16.5%, but the actual applicable tax rate depends on the type of entity and relevant regulations. If an individual receives compensation in crypto assets through work, such as receiving wages in USDT or other tokens, they may be subject to salaries tax. Hong Kong does not simply determine taxation based on the length of time a position is held, but rather on the nature of the transaction, business activities, and source of income. AKI: How is this assessed for Web3 companies registered in the BVI or Cayman Islands but with their actual teams located in Hong Kong? Calix: It requires consideration of the company's tax residency, the location of its business activities, and CARF reporting obligations. If a company is registered in an offshore jurisdiction but its actual management and operations primarily take place in Hong Kong, it may have a tax relationship with Hong Kong. Especially for cryptocurrency asset service providers, whether they need to fulfill CARF reporting obligations in Hong Kong cannot be determined solely by their place of registration or whether they have obtained a Hong Kong license; it also requires consideration of the RCASP definition and the Nexus Rules. However, CARF reporting obligations and whether a company needs to pay Hong Kong profits tax are not the same issue and must be analyzed separately. Where should mainland residents pay taxes after relocating to Hong Kong? AKI: If a mainland resident obtains Hong Kong residency and lives in Hong Kong long-term, which tax law should govern the income from crypto assets before and after the relocation? Calix: First, it's necessary to determine the individual's tax residency status. Obtaining Hong Kong residency does not automatically mean losing mainland tax residency status. Mainland tax law determines resident individuals based on factors such as domicile and length of residence. Tax-specific domicile requires consideration of household registration, family, and economic interests. Therefore, even if someone lives in Hong Kong long-term, they may still retain mainland tax residency status and be subject to corresponding reporting obligations.

Specifically, there may be situations where taxes are only paid in Hong Kong, or where tax returns are filed in both Hong Kong and mainland China. If double taxation exists, it needs to be handled in conjunction with the applicable tax arrangements and credit rules.

For crypto assets, the issue is more complex.

For example, receiving wages in the form of crypto assets, obtaining tokens through business activities, or converting investment income into fiat currency via OTC may involve different tax classifications.

Currently, there is still uncertainty regarding the specific tax treatment of different types of crypto asset income in mainland China, and it cannot be simply assumed that all crypto investment income is uniformly subject to a 20% tax rate.

There is still uncertainty regarding the specific tax treatment of different types of crypto asset income in mainland China, and it cannot be simply assumed that all crypto investment income is uniformly subject to a 20% tax rate.

Therefore, assets and income before and after relocating to Hong Kong need to be assessed separately based on the time of acquisition, the nature of income, and the tax residency status in both locations. Will withdrawals from Hong Kong bank cards be detected by the tax authorities if mainland China has not yet joined CARF? AKI: Mainland China has not yet joined CARF. If a mainland tax resident trades crypto assets in Hong Kong, will the relevant information be exchanged with the mainland? Calix: According to the current CARF participation arrangements, mainland China has not yet joined this information exchange framework. Therefore, relevant crypto asset transaction information will not be directly exchanged with the mainland through the CARF mechanism for the time being. However, this does not mean that all overseas financial information cannot be obtained, because CARF and CRS are two different systems. AKI: If crypto is exchanged for fiat currency via OTC and then transferred to a Hong Kong bank card, is it possible for mainland tax authorities to detect this? Calix: This involves CRS. If the tax residency of the Hong Kong bank account holder is identified as mainland China, the relevant account information may be exchanged with mainland tax authorities in accordance with CRS rules. The information exchanged through CRS typically includes the account holder's identity, account balance or value, and specific income and related amounts, but it does not mean that banks will automatically provide details of every cryptocurrency transaction. However, if tax authorities obtain information about overseas accounts through CRS and find a significant discrepancy between the account's funds and declared income, they may further inquire about the source of the funds. Therefore, even if cryptocurrency transaction information is not currently exchanged through CARF, once funds enter the traditional banking system, records that can be used for tax audits may still remain. Will mainland China retroactively examine historical Crypto income in the future? AKI: If mainland China strengthens tax regulation of crypto assets in the future, is it possible to retroactively apply investment income from the past few years? Calix: I think this possibility cannot be ruled out, but the specific timing, scope, and method are currently impossible to determine. Crypto assets have accumulated considerable wealth, and related income may come from investment, mining, staking, DeFi, token issuance, or other business activities. These activities may have different tax implications, and some may be subject to existing tax laws. Future regulation may first clarify the tax treatment of different crypto asset income through departmental regulations or policy interpretations, and then gradually improve the legal system. However, whether historical gains should be retroactively investigated, for how many years, and how to distinguish between ordinary underreporting and tax evasion all require specific legal provisions and cannot be concluded in advance. AKI: Which investors are likely to be the first to be audited by the tax authorities? Will they be screened based on asset size or trading frequency? Calix: It is currently impossible to make a reliable judgment. There are still many unclear aspects in the tax rules and actual collection methods for crypto assets in mainland China, and it is impossible to simply speculate that large investors, high-frequency traders, or certain types of practitioners will definitely be audited first. I think it is more important to keep records in advance, rather than guessing when the regulation will start or who will be audited first. What preparations should Web3 practitioners make before 2027? AKI: For Web3 practitioners and high-net-worth investors, what things should be addressed before the implementation of CARF in Hong Kong? Calix: I believe the first thing to change is one's attitude towards tax issues. As exchange KYC, anti-money laundering, and international tax information exchange systems gradually improve, crypto is entering a regulatory environment closer to traditional finance. Many investors in the past have not systematically organized their asset sources, transaction records, and tax status, which may lead to higher compliance costs in the future. For individuals holding substantial amounts of crypto assets, it is crucial to review the acquisition methods, historical transactions, fund flows, and relevant supporting documentation as early as possible, while also confirming their tax residency status in different regions. For Web3 companies, it is necessary to assess potential tax and reporting obligations based on actual business activities, company registration location, management team location, and business nature. If there are complex cross-border income, token compensation, or historical investment returns, professional tax advice can be sought in advance to explore applicable legal tax arrangements. The significance of CARF is not to require all crypto asset holders to pay a new tax, but rather to make it easier for tax authorities to obtain transaction information and determine tax obligations based on existing laws. Rather than waiting until information exchange begins to explain historical assets, it's better to establish complete asset and tax records in advance and make long-term plans while adhering to compliance.

data.title: Has the situation changed? Bessant "changes his tune": Huang Jen-hsun may be "unaware" of the situation.
data.description:
Author: Bao Yilong, Wall Street Insights

US Treasury Secretary Bessant hinted that the possibility of Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia has not been ruled out. This wording is significantly milder than his previous hardline stance calling for a "major overhaul" at Nvidia and seeking external leadership, leaving room for speculation about the founder's return.

On November 22, Bessant hinted in an interview with CBS's "Face the Nation" program that the possibility of Jensen Huang's return had not been ruled out, but emphasized that the government first needs to clarify the attribution of responsibility.

He said: "I think we need to see where the responsibility ultimately lies, and who the malicious perpetrators at the bottom of the company are." He also revealed that, as of November 22, the U.S. Treasury Department had not received a response from Nvidia regarding whether it had established shell companies to circumvent export controls; the deadline for a response was November 25. These remarks mark a shift in Bessant's tone. Just last week, he called for a “major overhaul” of Nvidia on Fox News and suggested that the next leader of the AI ​​chip giant should be chosen “from outside the company.” The prediction market has already reacted to this. On the Polymarket platform, the probability of Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia CEO has risen from 11% on November 21 to 14%.

Shift in Stance: From "External Succession" to "He's Already Outside"

Bessenter's change in stance is a key turning point in recent events.

Last week, he harshly criticized Nvidia on Fox News, calling for a "major restructuring" of the company and suggesting that the next leader of the AI ​​chip giant should come from "outside the company". This statement was interpreted by the market at the time as the Treasury Department not supporting Jensen Huang's return. However, in a CBS interview on November 22, when pressed about whether Nvidia should seek an external candidate to lead the company, Bessant responded: "I said they should look outside, but he's outside now." Bessant also emphasized that the chain of responsibility had not yet been clarified. He stated, "We need to see where the responsibility stops," and pressed for details, asking, "Is it at the bottom, the middle, or all the way to the top?" He expressed confidence that Nvidia's various committees would swiftly advance their investigations and believed they would provide a "robust and reliable" answer. The Board's Disagreements with the White House: Trump publicly supported Jensen Huang's return and called on the board to reinstate the co-founder from over 30 years ago. Huang's supporters also urged the board to reconsider his departure decision. This contrasts with the stance of Nvidia's board of directors, which has explicitly stated that it has no intention of bringing Huang back. Analysts believe that if the board insists on not bringing Huang back, its response to the government may be more inclined to place the blame on the former CEO; conversely, if the government accepts Huang's return, it may reduce some regulatory pressure. Bessant's statement keeps both paths open, but allegations surrounding Nvidia's compliance with China regulations remain unresolved. Last week, Bessant requested Nvidia to inform the Trump administration by November 25 whether it had established shell companies to circumvent export controls. He stated on November 22 that the U.S. Treasury Department had not yet received these responses.

data.title: Wrapped Monero Token Crashes 99.8% After Suspected $13.5M Private Key Exploit
data.description:
A suspected private key compromise has triggered a devastating collapse in a wrapped version of Monero (XMR), wiping out 99.8% of the token's value after approximately $13.5 million worth of XMR1 was sold on Hyperliquid.

包装门罗币XMR1 30分钟从500美元跌到1美元 跌99.8% 私钥放在云服务器 删了也白删 托管不等于自持 $XMR1 https://t.co/kNj1Tp5KPk

— 上车的乘客 (@chenke20266) November 22, 2026

The token, known as XMR1, plunged from around $500 to approximately $1 in just 30 minutes on Friday, according to blockchain analytics firm Bitquery. The investigation identified a wallet that received 5.2 million XMR1 tokens from the deployer account before selling approximately $13.5 million worth of the asset.

The incident has raised fresh concerns about the security of wrapped cryptocurrencies and the infrastructure responsible for issuing and managing them. Wagyu, the service behind XMR1, has blamed an alleged breach involving its hosting provider, while the exact circumstances surrounding the suspected private key compromise remain unclear.

Bitquery Traces $13.5M in XMR1 Sales Through Arbitrum and Ethereum

According to Bitquery's onchain investigation, the wallet that received 5.2 million XMR1 tokens from the deployer account proceeded to sell approximately $13.5 million worth of the wrapped cryptocurrency.

🚨 Suspected theft: the XMR1 deployer wallet on Hyperliquid sent 5.2M XMR1 to a newly funded address, which sold into the order book for ~$13.3M USDC. XMR1 fell from ~$494 to ~$1 in about 35 minutes. https://t.co/iylE3F7gBT

— Scam Sniffer (@realScamSniffer) November 20, 2026

The blockchain analytics firm traced approximately $13.28 million in USDC transferred to Arbitrum, where around $13.22 million was exchanged for 7,467 Ether through CoW Protocol. Most of the ETH was subsequently bridged to Ethereum.

Bitquery also identified approximately $6.6 million worth of XMR1 purchases funded by proceeds from four earlier November hacks involving Across Protocol, Kava, Lighter, and Safe. Those purchases appeared to be an attempt to obtain native Monero through the wrapped token.

However, Bitquery found no onchain evidence connecting those earlier security incidents to Friday's suspected exploit.

It is important to distinguish the affected asset from Monero itself. Wrapped tokens represent cryptocurrencies on other blockchain networks, allowing users to trade or access assets outside their native environments. In this case, XMR1 represents Monero through Wagyu's infrastructure and is traded on Hyperliquid.

The 99.8% collapse affected XMR1 rather than Monero's native XMR cryptocurrency, meaning the incident does not establish that Monero itself suffered a similar price collapse.

Wagyu Operator Blames Hosting Provider Breach for Suspected Key Compromise

PerpetualCow, the pseudonymous operator of Wagyu, attributed the incident to an alleged security breach involving hosting provider 1984, claiming that customer data and internal server files had been exposed.

Post-mortem of the $13m XMR hack: It's WORSE than I thought. Turns out that the entire hosting provider of https://t.co/aZzKk23eCg got hacked with everyone's data + internal server files today. The XMR1 deployer key was held on an OLD server on there that I DELETED, but somehow the logs/files were still kept. Lesson to learn here is that these hosting providers keep your data/logs even after you delete your server with them. Like I said before, everyone who lost money due to this will be refunded by me personally and Wagyu will re-launch at a later stage. Give me some time please.

— PerpetualCow.hl (@PerpetualCow) November 20, 2026

According to PerpetualCow, the private key associated with the XMR1 deployer account had been stored on a server that was subsequently deleted. However, the operator alleged that the hosting provider retained logs and files associated with the server, potentially exposing sensitive information.

The operator's explanation has not been independently confirmed. Bitquery said its investigation could not establish how the deployer account's private key was obtained or who controlled it during the suspicious transfers.

The analytics firm also noted that an alleged theft of the key from the hosting environment and a reported attack on the hosting provider do not establish where or how the private key was originally compromised.

Following the collapse, PerpetualCow pledged to personally reimburse affected traders and said Wagyu would eventually relaunch, although no specific timeline was provided.

Whoever was MMing XMR1 and lost money on it will be refunded fully obviously. Nobody will have lost money on this hack (except me 😢) Give me some time to cook and re-launch.

— PerpetualCow.hl (@PerpetualCow) November 20, 2026

The incident highlights the security risks surrounding wrapped cryptocurrencies, where users depend not only on the underlying digital asset but also on the infrastructure responsible for issuing and managing its wrapped counterpart.

Although Monero's native cryptocurrency was not directly affected, XMR1's near-total collapse demonstrates how a suspected compromise involving a deployer account can trigger severe consequences for traders.

With the circumstances surrounding the private key compromise still unresolved, questions remain about how the breach occurred, who was responsible, and whether Wagyu's operator will be able to fulfill the promised reimbursements.

data.title: Unveiling the truth behind Anthropic's "excessive profits": Caching tax
data.description:
These past two days, the AI ​​developer community has been blown up by a post that seems almost magical.

The poster was Vlad Mihalcea, a legendary figure in the Java world and a Java Champion winner ... AI developer community has been blown up by a post that seems almost magical these past two days.

The poster was Vlad Mihalcea, a legendary figure in the Java world and a Java Champion winner.

He stared at his Claude bill from the past year and posed the ultimate question: "I completely don't understand Anthropic's business model. My Pro plan only cost $200 a year, but I used up 16 billion tokens—if it were charged on a pay-as-you-go basis via API, that would be a whopping $100,000!" $100,000 worth of stuff, sold to you for $200? This isn't a tech company; this is clearly Silicon Valley's philanthropists using investors' money to give away charity. If you think this is just an extreme case of a hardcore programmer, then a recently released set of test data will only make you question your existence even more. On November 20, 2026, a hardcore user deduced the equivalent weekly token consumption of the three major AI subscriptions using real usage data: The $20/month Claude Pro plan (running Opus 5.5 + Claude Code) can consume approximately 818 million tokens per week; upgrading to the $200/month Claude Ultra or ChatGPT Pro directly increases the weekly token consumption to 8.18 billion and 9.385 billion respectively, even the relatively restrained Google AI Ultra 20X provides 5.164 billion. Semiconductor analysis firm SemiAnalysis even did the math: spending $200/month on a top-tier Claude subscription could yield up to $8,000/month in equivalent API usage, while OpenAI's figure was as high as $14,000/month—on paper, the vendors were losing 40 to 70 times more. Seeing this, many onlookers are starting to worry for Anthropic: How can they continue operating? Will their computing power collapse and they be delisted tomorrow? Amidst the heated discussion, Gergely Orosz, founder of the renowned technical newsletter *The Pragmatic Engineer*, offered his explanation: "Every software engineer must understand one thing: the first lesson in inference engineering is—reading from key-value caches is almost free, and speculative decoding dramatically increases the efficiency of long sessions. Programming scenarios precisely utilize these two technologies to their fullest potential. This is why AI inference is actually incredibly profitable!" [Image of an image] Wow, we thought we were frantically "fleecing" the system, but actually they were counting money until their hands cramped in the background! How exactly was this calculated? Today, we'll expose the profit-making logic behind Anthropic's business model.

The Illusion of 16 Billion Tokens:Coding Agent is a "Heavy Repeater"

To solve the case, we need to clarify one issue first: Were the 16 billion tokens burned by Vlad really all "original content" painstakingly typed out word by word by Claude?

Absolutely not.

Absolutely not.

In the early days of chatbots, you asked a question, and the AI ​​answered; token consumption increased linearly. But now, in the era of Coding Agents, the entire game has changed. A programming agent working is essentially a "repeater" in a crazy infinite loop: It first reads through the context of your entire codebase (assuming there are N tokens on the order of N times). The longer the session and the more frequently the tool is called, the more exponentially the total number of tokens explodes. Many developers have always assumed that the most expensive part of the bill is the high-priced "Output Tokens." Typesafe co-founder and CEO Diogo Almieda wrote a simulator to recreate the actual programming process of NVIDIA Open-SWE-Traces using the pricing of the Fable 5. The results showed that: Output Tokens, actually used to generate code and responses, only account for 9% to 18% of the total bill! Another developer, Martin Alderson, simulated a... An Opus 5 session with 60,000 token contexts and 100 rounds of dialogue revealed that approximately 76% of the bill was spent on "Cache Reads". In other words, in real-world programming agent scenarios, over 90% of token consumption actually involves the model repeatedly reading historical data it viewed just seconds prior. At this point, you might ask: even if it's repeatedly "rereading," that's still reading 16 billion tokens, doesn't the GPU consume a lot of power? How can this allow Anthropic to make a fortune? This is where the first real trump card comes in. Trump Card One: KV Cache, AI Vendors' "Zero Marginal Cost Money Printing Machine" Don't be intimidated by terms like "KV Cache." To understand the physical cost of large model inference, you only need to remember three things: The first step: Prefill – computationally expensive. When the model first reads your codebase, the GPU must perform numerous matrix operations at full capacity to convert the text into intermediate states (activation values) that the machine can understand, and then store them in video memory. This stored "reading notes" is the KV cache. Once the cache is written, the next time the same content is read, there is absolutely no need to recalculate. Step Two: Decoding – Consumes Significant Memory Bandwidth. When the model starts outputting tokens, for each token, the entire key-value cache (KV) must be retrieved from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for review. This step involves minimal computation but a massive amount of data transfer. This is why the output token price of various APIs is often 5 times higher than the input price – the memory bandwidth during the decoding stage is the real physical bottleneck for large model inference. Step 3: Tool Invocation – simply pressing the "pause button". When the Coding Agent stops to run a grep or execute a script, the previously calculated KV cache is quietly lying in memory. Letting a bunch of bytes lie in memory for a few seconds consumes neither computing power nor GPU bandwidth. Now, the most absurd and profitable scene unfolds. When the model generates output all at once, it reads the entire key-value cache for each generated character. The vendor doesn't charge an extra "cache read fee" because this overhead is already included in the expensive output unit price. However, once the Agent stops, calls a tool, and resumes, the API immediately becomes stern, charging a "cache read fee" based on the number of tokens, for the same key-value cache lying untouched in memory with almost zero computational cost. Diogo Almieda summed this up scathingly: The reason you still have to pay for KV caching after using the tool isn't due to any profound technical difficulties; it's simply because—"The vendor sets the price this way; take it or leave it." Anthropic itself inadvertently revealed this long ago. If you look through the Claude API documentation, you'll find a very intriguing detail: The tokens read from the cache are not taken into account for the API's input rate limit. (Limits)! Think about it, what is rate limiting for? It's used to protect servers from being overwhelmed by traffic. Anthropic's decision to exclude cache reads from rate limiting is like shouting to the world, "This doesn't take up much of my actual computing power, you can read as much as you want!" As for OpenAI, it ran its automatic prefix cache for free for over a year before adding cache writes in GPT-5.6, just like Anthropic. A 1.25x premium. Once this layer of secrecy is broken, the mystery of Vlad's $100,000 charge instantly becomes clear. That $100,000 is not Anthropic's true cost, but rather a figure calculated from its API pricing table, which is based on "layers of markups on almost free cache reads." For pay-as-you-go enterprise customers, programming agents... Each additional tool adjustment generates an additional "caching tax" for the vendor. This tax incurs almost no cost, naturally driving up inference profit margins. However, Anthropic waives this "caching tax" for subscribers paying $20 or $200 per month, allowing them to freely burn billions or even tens of billions of tokens. On paper, it seems like a loss of several times the initial investment, but the actual hardware cost incurred by the vendor is likely only a fraction of the listed price. However, even a fraction is still money. SemiAnalysis' October estimate showed that subscriptions only contribute a small percentage to Anthropic's revenue. It accounts for about 10% of revenue but consumes over 40% of the inference computing power. Heavy users who max out their plans often end up losing money on it. **Second trump card: Speculative decoding – squeezing every last drop of GPU time** If KV caching has driven down the cost of "input reading," then how does Anthropic save money and speed up the real physical bottleneck mentioned earlier – the "output" decoding stage? This is where Gergely Orosz comes in. The second trump card has been revealed: Speculative Decoding. As mentioned earlier, when the model decodes words, it mainly gets stuck on memory bandwidth, causing the extremely expensive computing cores inside the GPU to be in a "laid-off" state most of the time. It's like a Michelin-starred chef standing in front of the stove, spending 90% of the time waiting for the prep cook to bring the dishes. Speculative decoding does exactly that—completely squeezes out all the chef's downtime. The manufacturer will equip a very fast small model (or a dedicated predictor) next to the large model as a "stenographer," allowing it to blindly guess the next few tokens in one go. Then, it will package these tokens and feed them to the large model, which will use its idle computing power to simultaneously verify the accuracy of the guesses in a single forward computation. If the guesses are correct, they are all allowed to proceed; if incorrect, they are sent back for rewriting. Which scenario do you think is best suited for "blind guessing"? Writing poetry wouldn't work, because the poet's next line might be wildly imaginative; but writing code is a perfect match! The code is full of highly predictable structure: fixed syntax parentheses, recurring variable names, function signatures copied from the context, minor refactoring modifications to existing code... The small model guesses the code with incredible accuracy, achieving a shockingly high acceptance rate. The result is that code that previously required five or six memory transfers can now be processed in a single transfer. Now, putting the two cards together, a perfect and impressive business puzzle emerges: Input relies on KV caching: Agent Frenzied rereading of context? Almost zero computational cost, API still charges caching fees, subscription model easily provides extremely high limits; Output relies on speculative decoding: Code is highly predictable, using idle computing power to maximize generation speed and throughput, further reducing the real cost per session. Even though large-scale models are becoming increasingly commercialized and open-source models are closing in, the gross profit margin of inference in cutting-edge labs is actually getting higher and higher. The secret lies here. After seeing through the cards, who is winning and who is paying the price? After dissecting this "inference economics," when we look back at the current AI landscape, many seemingly contradictory phenomena instantly become clear, and the coping strategies of different roles are actually quite distinct. First, if you are an ordinary individual developer, don't hesitate, continuing to happily "take advantage" of subscription packages is the most cost-effective deal. Whether it's the $200 Pro plan for a year or the $200 top-tier plan for a month, manufacturers are exchanging your long-term retention and ecosystem stickiness for extremely low marginal costs—a rare win-win situation. Next time you see billions of tokens in your backend statistics, you can smile knowingly. If you're a technical team working on AI Agents, beware of the "Smart Routing" pitfall! Many teams, to save money, like to add a router to their Agent: [The text then abruptly shifts to a seemingly unrelated topic about sending difficult problems to a router.] Opus, a simple step to switch to the cheaper Sonnet. Sounds smart? Actually, it's incredibly costly. Because KV caches cannot be shared between different models! A practical calculation shows that in an Opus 5 session with 100,000 token contexts, even if the next step only requires generating 1,000 tokens, if you switch to the cheaper model midway, you're forced to rewrite all 100,000 contexts from scratch into the new model's cache—resulting in the "cost-saving operation" actually increasing the cost of this step by nearly 3 times. This resulted in an even less efficient model. Here's a counterintuitive conclusion: For long-context coding agents, the cheapest model may not perform the cheapest task. The real cost isn't just the model's unit price, but also how much cache is wasted with each switch. A truly effective, cost-saving architecture involves having subagents handle the dirty work that doesn't inherit the main context (like searching through 50,000 tokens' logs and extracting only 200 words to report to the main agent), controlling the main context's expansion at its source. Finally, for enterprises running agents on a large scale, the trend of open-source self-deployment is unstoppable. As Diogo Almieda pointed out, if enterprises run massive amounts of agents using APIs every day, they are essentially handing over the huge cost benefits brought by KV caching to closed-source vendors. This is why, in the past year, a large number of tech giants have decisively "fled" closed-source APIs: Uber reduced the cost per token by 50% through architectural optimization, AT&T by 56%, and Pinterest by a staggering 90%; fintech giant Revolut simply purchased 56 Nvidia B200 bare-metal servers to run them themselves. More and more teams are using professional inference clouds like Modal, Fireworks, and Baseten to run open-source weighted models such as DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3, and Kimi K3.1 Pro—only by controlling the inference stack can they keep the money saved from KV caching. The good news is that the exorbitant "caching tax" is starting to show signs of loosening. Recently, Fable 5.1 drastically reduced its cache read price from $1 per million tokens to $0.25. And that's not all. On November 9th, Fable 5.2 was released, further reducing the cache read price to $0.20. In just over two months, cache read prices have dropped by a full 80% compared to the Fable 5 era. Even more intriguing is that Anthropic itself admits that simply reducing cache read prices could potentially lower the overall cost of complex programming and agent tasks by up to approximately 45%. This demonstrates that for coding agents that frequently invoke tools and repeatedly read context, caching is no longer a dispensable optimization, but a key variable determining the overall cost. As reasoning engineering has completely transformed from "black box magic" into essential knowledge for software engineers, the period of lucrative profits from information asymmetry will eventually come to an end.

data.title: OpenAI has just released its core pre-training metrics for the first time.
data.description:
As AI becomes increasingly powerful, OpenAI is calling for an "upper limit" for the entire industry. On November 22nd, local time, OpenAI's Chief Scientist, Jakub Pachocki, suddenly published a lengthy article, "Perplexity and Intelligence," publicly revealing a set of internal pre-training metrics and proposing a controversial suggestion: the world's leading AI companies should jointly agree on an upper limit for model development. Before AI safety monitoring capabilities reach a certain standard, no company should cross this line. This time, OpenAI even proactively disclosed data that its competitors have been eager to know. Pachocki chose a metric called Perplexity. It measures a model's ability to predict the next token; the lower the value, the more accurate the prediction. According to data disclosed by OpenAI, GPT-3.5 has a logarithmic perplexity of approximately 0.99, and GPT-4 has approximately 0.91. When this number drops below 0.8, the model begins to demonstrate breakthrough capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics; at approximately 0.76, the model is already able to solve some long-standing mathematical problems. More alarmingly, Pachocki believes that AI may soon begin to accelerate its own research and development. As early as 2027, pre-training algorithm research may see a fundamental breakthrough, while security monitoring technology may not be able to keep up at the same pace. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also publicly stated that this is one of the most important announcements OpenAI has made recently. OpenAI is significantly increasing the transparency of pre-training progress and hopes that the entire industry can reach a consensus on common limitations. In Altman's view, this is a very wise approach, helping to ensure the safety and controllability of AI.

The following is the original compilation of Jakub Pachocki:

data.title: Galaxy Digital: Solana's Institutionalization Tipping Point
data.description:
Author: Lucas Tcheyan, VP of Research, Galaxy Digital; Translator: Shaw, Jinse Finance

Event Recap

Solana's annual flagship conference, Breakpoint, was held in London from November 15th to 17th, with the theme "Token Supercycle," showcasing the public chain's increasingly ambitious plans in payments, tokenization, and institutional finance.

This conference also marked Solana's official departure from the "mainnet beta" version and its upgrade to Mainnet 1.0.

Leveraging a series of infrastructure upgrades and the Alpenglow consensus protocol, the network's target block time has been halved to 200 milliseconds, and the final transaction confirmation time has been compressed to approximately 150 milliseconds. Institutional adoption was a core focus of the conference's announcements. Zelle, a bank-affiliated payment network (processing over $1.2 trillion in transactions by 2025), demonstrated a confidential $1.25 million stablecoin transfer and announced plans to launch ZelleUSD on Solana for cross-border payments. Global remittance giant MoneyGram and wallet service provider Solflare jointly launched USDC cash-to-cash services covering 170 countries and regions; fintech lending platform SoFi listed Solana as its preferred public chain for stablecoins and tokenized assets. Tokenization was another major theme. The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) disclosed plans to integrate its tokenized services into Solana in the second half of 2027. Wealth management platform Allfunds, banking giant BNY Mellon, and asset management firm Baillie Gifford also announced several plans to bring traditional investment products onto the blockchain. Other announcements covered tokenized stocks, regulated derivatives, decentralized computing power, and smart agent payments, reflecting Solana's attempt to expand beyond its original strengths—retail trading and decentralized finance—and broaden its boundaries. Our Viewpoint: Since 2023, Solana's evolution has created a growing gap between the market's preconceived notions of it and the actual goals the ecosystem aims to achieve. For casual observers, Solana remains associated with Meme coin speculation and the ensuing gray market activities. However, market participants who closely monitor the ecosystem see that this public chain is continuously positioning itself as the underlying infrastructure for payments, tokenized assets, and other financial activities, potentially bringing a much larger scale of users and funds onto the chain. These two positioning strategies are not mutually exclusive. Solana's success as an "on-chain casino" was a powerful engine attracting users, developers, liquidity, and capital. It possesses the ability to handle large-scale, high-frequency, small-amount financial transactions, building a competitive advantage in a market where speed, cost, and ease of use are sufficient for success. However, the conditions supporting Solana's leadership in this field are fundamentally different from the underlying logic adopted by institutions in the next stage. Payments, tokenization, and smart agent commerce continue to attract the attention of leading global financial institutions, payment service providers, and technology companies. These players possess resources and channels far exceeding those of native crypto startups; Solana is just one of many public chains they are considering, and they also have the ability to develop and control their own proprietary infrastructure. For institutions, performance is increasingly becoming an entry barrier, rather than a differentiating advantage. Privacy, compliance, operational accountability, channel reach, and access to liquidity pools are all equally important. Therefore, at least in the short term, Solana's real opportunity lies not in becoming a universal settlement layer for global finance, but in becoming a leading neutral settlement for a type of financial activity—activities suited to operating on shared, composable, and high-performance public infrastructure. A recent paper published by JPMorgan's Kinexys and MIT's Digital Currency Institute highlights this contradiction. The paper states that financial institutions recognize the value of public blockchains as shared infrastructure not controlled by a single entity; however, institutional requirements for confidentiality, compliance, governance, and other operational aspects conflict with the core characteristics of public blockchains themselves. To meet institutional needs, it is often necessary to reintroduce intermediaries, access control, and centralized control, which may weaken the core value of public blockchains that distinguishes them from traditional systems: neutrality and interoperability. Building a private blockchain also presents its own challenges, especially in scenarios where multiple competing institutions need to collaborate across fragmented systems. Ultimately, it's highly unlikely that there will be a complete migration from private infrastructure to public chains. Instead, public chains will be adopted gradually and selectively in scenarios where their advantages are sufficiently prominent. This Breakpoint conference simultaneously showcased both opportunities and limitations. Zelle's confidential transfer demonstration, DTCC's integration plans, and projects from leading asset management institutions indicate that institutions are considering Solana as an alternative financial business solution beyond crypto-native solutions. Its share of tokenized stock trading also proves that this chain can attract effective traffic from emerging asset classes. From January to September 2026, Solana handled approximately 42% of on-chain tokenized stock trading volume. However, being "selected as a supporting public chain" and "becoming the core venue for the final accumulation of liquidity, users, and economic activity" are two different things. For example, DTCC's integration is part of its broader multi-chain strategy, not an exclusive commitment to Solana. Furthermore, Solana will face competition from crypto-native products as it enters these sectors. Hyperliquid remains a strong player in the on-chain perpetual derivatives market; in the emerging agent economy, there is still no clear winner, and there is no strong reason to believe that payment and collaboration infrastructure will necessarily concentrate on Solana. While privacy tools are iterating, maturity, regulatory compliance, and institutional adoption remain unresolved issues. Against this backdrop, the ecosystem's ability to retain developers is crucial. A high-density developer culture and an environment conducive to continuous experimentation are key to Solana's recovery from the bear market and its continued growth; retaining these qualities is equally important in the phase of attracting institutional funding. Solana has made significant progress in fixing the technical shortcomings that previously damaged its credibility. The more challenging task is translating technological advancements into stable channels, liquidity, and institutional reliance—in this type of market, performance alone is rarely enough to determine success. Breakpoint proves that Solana has secured its place in this game. But the more crucial question is whether it can stand out from the numerous options and establish a long-term, stable advantage, rather than merely serving as a backup option in the increasingly competitive multi-chain financial system.

data.title: Trump blames the market sell-off on Democrats; Bessant says multiple factors contributed.
data.description:
Author: Xiao Yanyan, Jinshi Data

The US stock market has recently experienced a sharp sell-off, with President Trump pointing the finger at the Democratic Party, believing that their victory in the November 3 midterm elections was the main reason for the market's sharp decline.

Trump posted on the social media platform Truth Social on Sunday: "Since that rather strange 'victory' of the Democrats on November 3, the stock market has fallen by more than $6 trillion. The Nasdaq alone has fallen by 20%. This is 100% because the Democrats are 'terrible,' pursuing anti-growth, retaliatory policies, and it's going to get worse."

He also warned that if the Democrats do not quickly change their policies, the market could weaken further.However, Trump stated that the US economy will soon recover strongly. “Our country will soon be strong again—and many good things will happen,” he concluded. The recent decline in U.S. stocks has reached a level rarely seen in history. According to Yahoo Finance, as of last Friday's close, U.S. stocks experienced a similar drop, occurring only five times since World War II, with 2008 and 2001 being particularly notable examples. The Nasdaq Composite Index has continued to decline after hitting a record high in early October, and its year-to-date gains have turned negative. As of last Friday, the index was down more than 4,700 points from its all-time closing high of 27,599.886 points on October 6. Technology stocks have faced even greater pressure. According to Yahoo Finance, chip stocks experienced their worst week since September 2001, just one week after the September 11 terrorist attacks. Nvidia (NVDA.O) was not spared either. Since its stock price peaked on October 6, the company's market capitalization has evaporated by approximately $2.7 trillion. Bessent: Multiple Factors Triggered the Sell-Off U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent did not simply attribute the market decline to the election results, but rather believed that multiple factors contributed to the sell-off. In an interview with Margaret Brennan on CBS's "Face the Nation" on Sunday, Bessant stated that the market sell-off actually began when polls showed Democrats leading and accelerated further after Election Day. He specifically mentioned the Democrats' stance on artificial intelligence infrastructure development. Bessant stated, "The Democrats' position on superintelligence (SI) development has worried many investors, who fear it will slow down the development process." Here, "superintelligence" is Trump's preferred term for artificial intelligence. Bessant believes that the Democrats' potential for increased regulation of the AI ​​industry, particularly restrictions on data center construction, has already affected investors' assessment of the industry's future. Federal Reserve policy is another source of pressure. Bessant stated, "We've also heard some very hawkish comments from the Fed. Many believe that if the Fed tightens monetary policy too much, it could make a policy mistake." As market expectations for further interest rate hikes rise, tech companies are facing increasing financing costs and valuation pressures. AI regulation and the Nvidia controversy exacerbate pressure on tech stocks. Technology analyst Dan Ives described the recent predicament of tech stocks as a "perfect storm." He believes that after the Democrats' landslide victory in the midterm elections, the market began to worry about increased government regulation of the artificial intelligence and data center industries, leading some investors to reassess the prospects for AI infrastructure investment. The leadership change at Nvidia also exacerbated market anxiety. Following the departure of CEO Jensen Huang, investors are concerned about whether Nvidia can continue to provide crucial support for the entire AI industry ecosystem. Meanwhile, Nvidia is also facing multiple investigations regarding whether the company made false statements to investors and violated US export control regulations. Ives believes that the simultaneous emergence of AI industry regulatory risks, changes in Nvidia's management, and market anxieties about tech stocks has exacerbated this round of sell-offs. From Trump blaming the stock market decline on the Democrats to Bessant emphasizing Federal Reserve policies and AI regulatory risks, the White House's explanations for the market correction are not entirely the same. However, it is certain that after the Democrats' midterm election victory, AI industry policies and the prospects for data center construction have become important factors for investors to reassess tech stocks.
